items.headline: K-Pop’s Big Four Establish FANOMENON Company Ahead of 2027 Festival
items.dek: HYBE, SM, JYP and YG have joined forces on a company for the K-culture event planned across Seoul and Goyang in December 2027.
body: HYBE, SM Entertainment, JYP Entertainment and YG Entertainment have established a joint venture for FANOMENON, bringing four of K-pop’s largest agencies together ahead of the planned December 2027 festival.

FANOMENON Co., Ltd. was registered on October 26, 2026, according to corporate registry information reported by The Korea Herald. The company will oversee the event’s planning, production and operation, marking a step forward for a project the agencies began preparing earlier this year.

The inaugural FANOMENON is scheduled for December 2–12, 2027, at Seoul Arena in Seoul and KINTEX in Goyang, Gyeonggi Province. According to Korea.net, the plan combines K-pop concerts and fandom awards with exhibitions and interactive programs from Korean culture companies.

At Seoul Arena, the awards are envisioned as a mix of performances and honors for fan communities, with artists accepting awards on their fans’ behalf. KINTEX is planned to host multi-artist performances alongside exhibitions and hands-on experiences.

The Korea Herald reports that FANOMENON Co. launched with 4 billion won in paid-in capital. Park Yun-suh, who previously worked at HYBE and JYP, will serve as CEO, while each of the four participating agencies has a non-executive director on the board.

The company’s stated business scope extends beyond staging performances to areas including ticket sales, venue operating rights, merchandise and intellectual-property licensing. Its formation follows an April announcement by the agencies that they were preparing a collaborative company to advance the event.

The FANOMENON name combines “fan” and “phenomenon.” The project has also drawn scrutiny over its trademark, which JYP initially filed. The Korea Herald reports that a revised agreement submitted to the National Assembly divides the rights equally between the Culture Ministry and the joint venture.

items.headline: ILLIT scores first Billboard 200 top 10 with ‘BREAK EVEN’

body: ILLIT has landed its first top 10 album on the Billboard 200, as “BREAK EVEN” debuts at No. 6 on the U.S. chart dated November 14.
The mini album also opens at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Album Sales chart, marking the group’s first release to lead the sales ranking, Soompi reported.

According to Luminate, “BREAK EVEN” earned 37,000 equivalent album units in the United States during the week ending November 5. That total included 32,500 traditional album sales, ILLIT’s biggest U.S. sales week to date, and 4,500 streaming equivalent album units. The latter represented 4.87 million on-demand audio streams.
The Billboard 200 ranks albums using a combination of sales and streaming activity, while Top Album Sales measures album sales. Billboard announced the new chart results on November 8.

“BREAK EVEN” is ILLIT’s fifth Billboard 200 entry and surpasses the group’s previous peak of No. 26 with “MAMIHLAPINATAPAI.” Their other entries were “SUPER REAL ME,” which reached No. 93; “I’LL LIKE YOU,” which peaked at No. 94; and “bomb,” which reached No. 171.

body: Red Velvet's Joy and Kim Hyun Jin are set to begin their romance on the wrong foot in "One-of-a-Kind Romance," which releases its first two episodes on November 9 at 6 p.m. KST.

Joy plays Gong Yu Il, a college graduate trying to find a job while working to support herself. Even on the day of an interview, she takes a night shift at a convenience store. There, she meets customer Tak Mu I, a top star played by Kim Hyun Jin.

The pair cross paths again at a filming location, but what feels like coincidence to Yu Il looks more suspicious to Mu I. With a stalker already weighing on him, he starts watching her closely. When he spots her on set, he exchanges a telling glance with his manager, Kim Young Soo, played by Choi Kwon.

Yu Il's friend Yoo Yeon Joo, a drama production PD played by Na Hyun Young, also appears in the opening episodes. Yu Il eventually becomes Mu I's manager, bringing the two closer as they develop a relationship. Mu I, who carries emotional scars from the stalking incident, once found strength in a novel Yu Il wrote years earlier.
Based on a Naver webtoon by Dubu, the drama is directed by Kim Jin Young and written by Jeon Hyun Mi. The first two episodes will be available on TVING, Viu and Japan's ABEMA.

body: SEVENTEEN have taken on everything from deceptive quizzes to zombies on GOING SEVENTEEN. In a new watch list, Soompi recommends seven installments that show the range of the group’s variety series.

“Going Rangers” flips the superhero premise: the members compete to avoid becoming the universe’s savior. The cast and production crew join in the comedy, with moments including a spider dance and a Pikachu impression.
For fans who prefer strategy, “LIAR LIAR” turns a quiz into a contest of deception. Rather than simply getting answers right, the members try to mislead one another about what is true.

“SEVENTEEN TV” brings the group into a trainee-style dorm for a two-part series made as part of promotions for their 10th-anniversary album, HAPPY BURSTDAY. The members play exaggerated characters as they reenact trainee life.

In “MC BOO’s Dangerous Invitation,” Seungkwan interviews DK while the other members face a watery penalty whenever DK says an assigned forbidden word. Once he catches on, DK starts repeating the trigger words.

“WATER BATTLEGROUNDS” sends the members into a water-gun survival game, while “Mafiapoly” combines mafia and Monopoly with three members absent. Viewers sensitive to first-person camera footage may want to take care with “WATER BATTLEGROUNDS.”

body: Bleecker Street's event cinema division Crosswalk and Universal Pictures Content Group have picked up 'Twice: This Is For… You,' the concert film built around TWICE's night at London's O2 Arena. Crosswalk takes North American rights, while Universal handles the film internationally.

The film pairs concert footage from the 'This Is For' world tour with behind-the-scenes access and new interviews with the nine members, and it is set for a worldwide theatrical release on February 5, 2027, including IMAX screenings.

Paul Dugdale and Hannah Lux Davis directed the film, which was produced by Live Nation Studios. Crosswalk will release it in the United States and Canada, with Universal Pictures International handling cinemas in other territories.

The deal continues a partnership that already delivered 'Stray Kids: The dominATE Experience' earlier this year. The 'This Is For' tour itself was one of TWICE's biggest, running 44 cities and 81 shows from its July 2025 opening at Incheon Inspire Arena to its finale at Seoul's KSPO Dome in July 2026.
It is a separate project from 'Twice: One In A Million,' the documentary marking the group's 10th anniversary that was announced during the tour's opening shows.

items.headline: K-Pop Trade Organization Responds Amid NewJeans Contract Controversy
items.dek: The Korea Popmusic Industry Association has answered the New York Times' report on NewJeans' contracts, calling it one-sided and biased.
body: The Korea Popmusic Industry Association has answered the New York Times' report on NewJeans' contracts, calling the coverage a one-sided and biased assessment in a statement of more than 800 words issued on November 9.

The Times reported on November 5 that it had obtained the exclusive contracts the five members signed with ADOR in 2022, when they were aged 14 to 17. The paper said the deals left out protections for minors' education, health, sleep and rest that appear in the government's standard contract, and included limits on relationships and criticism of the company, steep exit penalties, and rights to keep using the members' names, likenesses and AI-generated voices after the contracts end in 2029.

The association, whose members include HYBE, SM, JYP and YG, argued that the report judged the deals by individual clauses alone, without weighing supplementary agreements, Korean law, or how the contracts were actually carried out. It pointed to the government's standard contract for popular culture artists and the Popular Culture and Arts Industry Development Act as the framework that protects both companies and artists.

It also said major companies sign the government's standard supplementary agreement for minors with every trainee, covering sleep, education and rest, and appoint youth protection officers. The group described the trainee system as a distinctive model that should not be judged through a Western lens, and raised concern that contract terms under confidentiality obligations were disclosed to foreign media while legal proceedings are still ongoing.
items.socialCaption: The K-pop industry's trade body has fired back at the NYT's NewJeans contract report, calling it a one-sided take on how the industry works.
items.seoDescription: KPIA has responded to the New York Times' report on NewJeans' ADOR contracts, defending the deals as lawful and the K-pop training system as a model in its own right.

items.headline: ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Directors Join Animated Short ‘Living With a Visionary’
items.dek: Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans have joined Stephen P. Neary's animated documentary short as executive producers, ahead of its premiere through The New York Times Op-Docs.
body: Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans, the directors behind KPop Demon Hunters, have joined the animated documentary short Living With a Visionary as executive producers. The short, narrated by James Cromwell, premieres through The New York Times Op-Docs this week.

Written, directed and animated by Stephen P. Neary, the film adapts a memoir by poet John Matthias. It follows his decades-long marriage to art curator Diana Matthias and how their life together shifts after her Parkinson's diagnosis, including the vivid hallucinations brought on by her medication, which John, now her caregiver, learns to live with alongside her.

Neary made the film with producer Mireia Vilanova, drawing thousands of illustrations by hand on layered vellum over three years, working on it during evenings and weekends around a full-time job and a teaching post at the California Institute of the Arts. The short has already picked up the grand jury prize for animation at AFI Fest and the short film jury award for animation at Sundance earlier this year.

Neary previously created and ran The Fungies! for Cartoon Network and HBO Max, supervised production on the Annie-nominated Clarence, and worked as a story artist on KPop Demon Hunters, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs, Rio and The Peanuts Movie. Kang and Appelhans said they were drawn to the project despite how different it looks from their own film, and Neary said the two projects share the same concerns underneath. Living With a Visionary is one of nine titles on Op-Docs' 2026 slate being talked about as awards contenders.

items.headline: Korean Organizations Reject Claim of Oppressive Control in K-Pop
items.dek: Korea's music industry association says the K-pop system is dedicated management and investment, not oppressive control.
body: A leading Korean music industry body has pushed back on the idea that K-pop runs on oppressive control, after a New York Times report on NewJeans' contracts put the industry's training system under the spotlight. The Korea Popmusic Industry Association said the description dismisses a system built on dedicated management and upfront investment.

In a statement on November 9, the association argued that the Times report, which said the 2022 ADOR contracts omitted youth protections and kept the company's rights over members' names, likenesses and AI-generated voices after the deals end, judged K-pop through a Western lens instead of on its own terms.

The group said major companies run artist care programs, some with in-house medical staff, and sign the government's standard supplementary agreements for minors, covering sleep, education and rest. Fairness, it argued, has to be judged with those agreements and Korean law in view, not clause by clause.

It also objected to contract details from an ongoing legal dispute being disclosed to foreign media despite confidentiality obligations, warning that one dispute was being stretched into a verdict on the whole industry. HYBE and ADOR had responded a day earlier, saying the contracts were lawful and negotiated in good faith.
items.socialCaption: K-pop's industry body says don't call it 'oppressive control', its new statement defends the training system behind the music.
items.seoDescription: The Korea Popmusic Industry Association has rejected the idea that K-pop is defined by oppressive control, pushing back on the New York Times' NewJeans contract report.

body: The Bias List has weighed in on NCT Dream's 'Boogie Woogie,' giving the title track an 8 out of 10 and a B- grade, a warm verdict for the group's bright, bubblegum return.

The review notes that this is the group's first project since founding member Mark Lee left to go solo, and that the song takes NCT Dream back to their upbeat roots, leaning on the members' polished skills to sell a sound that gets harder to carry as a group grows older.

The reviewer found the track openly cheesy, radio-friendly pop in the vein of BTS's 'Permission to Dance', but said its distinctly K-pop sparkle keeps it from sounding generic. The big chorus is both the hook that pulls listeners in and the part with the most cringe-worthy lyrics.

The moments around the chorus won the most praise: a post-chorus with a lighter lift, and short rap verses that ride the groove instead of trying to reinvent it. The reviewer wondered whether such a light song suits a 10th-anniversary release, but concluded it is hard to dislike a track that bursts with energy at every turn.
'Boogie Woogie' leads NCT Dream's sixth album, 'DREAM AFTER DREAM,' released on November 9, with album opener 'The Sun' pre-released last month.

items.headline: K-Pop Industry Pushes Back After NewJeans Contract Details Emerge
items.dek: After the New York Times published details of NewJeans' ADOR contracts, the K-pop industry body answered back.
body: The K-pop industry has pushed back after details of NewJeans' contracts with ADOR came to light, with the Korea Popmusic Industry Association calling the New York Times' report a one-sided and biased assessment.

The Times reported on November 5 that it had obtained the contracts the five members signed in April 2022, when they were aged 14 to 17. The paper said the deals dropped language from the government's standard contract protecting minors' education and physical and mental health, and gave the agency rights to keep using the members' names, likenesses and AI-generated voices after the contracts expire in 2029. One Seoul entertainment lawyer who reviewed the documents described the terms as unusually aggressive.

HYBE and ADOR answered the next day, saying the contracts were legal and negotiated in good faith, that the government template is a nonbinding guideline, and that the members' parents had accepted the changes. ADOR also said the members signed the standard supplementary agreements for minors, and that any AI use needs each artist's individual consent.

The industry association weighed in on November 9, saying a single contract dispute was being stretched into a structural verdict on the whole industry, and that fairness must be judged with supplementary agreements, Korean law and actual practice in view. It also objected to confidential contract terms being disclosed to foreign media while legal proceedings continue.
The dispute itself goes back to 2024, when the members announced they were ending their ADOR contracts; a Seoul court later upheld the contracts' validity.
items.socialCaption: The NewJeans contract story isn't over, the K-pop industry body has now responded to the NYT report, and HYBE and ADOR already answered too.

items.headline: HYBE Responds to New York Times Report on NewJeans Contracts
items.dek: HYBE and ADOR say the leaked NewJeans agreements were negotiated in good faith and are being used to attack the K-pop industry.
body: HYBE and its subsidiary ADOR have responded to a New York Times report on the exclusive contracts signed by the members of NewJeans in 2022. The Times reported on November 5 that it had obtained copies of the agreements, which the five members signed when they were aged between 14 and 17.

According to the paper, the contracts left out protections from South Korea's government contract template covering minors' rights to education, sleep, rest, and physical and mental health. The report also said the contracts barred an insincere attitude and inappropriate romantic relationships, and stopped members from publicly stating true or false facts that could damage ADOR's reputation. It also reported that ADOR could use and license the members' names, likenesses, and voices after the agreements expire in 2029, including through AI-generated voice clones or chatbots, and that members had to cover a significant share of the label's spending on cosmetic surgery and other beauty treatments while they were trainees.

In a statement sent to Music Business Worldwide on November 6, HYBE and ADOR said the contracts had been leaked to international media outlets and were being used as a means to attack the K-pop industry. The companies said every HYBE label signs the government-standard supplementary agreement for minors with its trainees, covering personal rights and the rights to sleep, education, and rest until they reach adulthood, and that the exclusive contracts themselves contain further provisions protecting fundamental rights.

HYBE said the draft contract was first shared on January 7, 2022, followed by extensive discussions before the contracts were signed in April that year, including written questions and answers, email correspondence, and negotiations over proposed revisions reviewed by the artists' legal counsel. The company also pointed to a Seoul High Court decision that recognised the contracts were made after sufficient discussions between the parties.

On the exit-penalty formula flagged by the Times, HYBE said the wording may look different from the government's standard contract, but the two provisions have the same economic effect, because only the pre-debut period is excluded. The clause is at issue in ADOR's lawsuit against former member Danielle Marsh, whose contract the label ended in December 2025, with ADOR seeking roughly 33.1 billion won, around 25 million US dollars, down from an initial 43.1 billion won. HYBE also named former ADOR chief Min Hee-jin as the person who led the contract process, a claim her representatives have disputed, saying HYBE's legal team drafted and revised the contracts.
items.socialCaption: HYBE and ADOR have answered the New York Times report on the NewJeans contracts, defending how the 2022 agreements were negotiated. Here's what each side is saying.
items.seoDescription: HYBE and ADOR push back on a New York Times report on the NewJeans contracts, saying the agreements were negotiated and the leak is being used against K-pop.

items.headline: K-Pop Association Challenges New York Times Report on NewJeans Contracts
items.dek: The Korea Popmusic Industry Association says the report turned one group's contract dispute into a judgment on the whole K-pop industry.
body: The Korea Popmusic Industry Association has pushed back on a recent New York Times report about NewJeans' contract, calling it a one-sided and biased assessment that overlooked Korea's legal safeguards for artist contracts and the value of the industry's artist development system.

In a statement on Monday, the association said it regretted that the newspaper had taken the controversy around an individual contract and treated it as a structural problem for the K-pop industry as a whole, without giving enough weight to regulatory progress and the industry's own efforts to improve its practices.

The association pointed to the Korean government's Standard Exclusive Contract for Popular Culture Artists and the Popular Culture and Arts Industry Development Act, saying both help protect the entertainment companies that invest in artists and the artists who can be in a relatively vulnerable position. It said companies and artists work together under that framework to discuss, draft, and agree on contract terms, and that protecting artists' rights has long been addressed through sustained work by companies and the government.

It also argued that the fairness and legality of an exclusive contract cannot be judged from individual clauses alone. Instead, it said, supplementary agreements, applicable laws, the circumstances around how the contract was entered into, and whether the obligations were actually fulfilled all need to be considered together. The group warned that judging a contract any other way risks spreading a distorted view of the industry and unfairly undermining the trust it has built over many years.

The association explained that major K-pop agencies, including HYBE, sign the government's standard supplementary agreement for minors with all their trainees, with provisions protecting their personal rights and their rights to sleep, education, and rest. It added that member companies have designated youth protection officers under the law, and that major companies run comprehensive artist care programs, in some cases employing in-house medical professionals. The trainee system, it said, is a distinctive model that should not be judged through a Western lens or dismissed as oppressive control. The group also raised concern that details from a contract at the centre of an ongoing legal dispute had been disclosed despite confidentiality obligations.
items.socialCaption: A K-pop industry association says the New York Times report on NewJeans missed Korea's legal safeguards for artists. Here's their side of the story.

items.headline: K-pop industry group challenges New York Times report on artist contracts
items.dek: The industry group says the report generalised one group's dispute and did not give enough weight to Korea's contract laws and trainee system.
body: A major K-pop industry association has criticised a recent New York Times report examining NewJeans' contract with label ADOR, arguing that the article unfairly generalised a dispute involving one group into a broader indictment of the K-pop industry.

The Korea Popmusic Industry Association said on Monday that it was deeply concerned by the report, which analysed the contract signed between NewJeans and ADOR when the bandmates were minors. The association, whose members include major entertainment companies such as HYBE, SM, JYP, and YG, argued that the report did not sufficiently consider Korea's legal framework for entertainment contracts or the characteristics of the K-pop trainee system.

The Times reported on Thursday that the contract contained a number of provisions that legal experts viewed as unfavourable to the signees, including the absence of clauses specifically protecting minors' rights to health, education, sleep, and rest. According to the report, the contract also addressed cosmetic procedure costs, restrictions on members' conduct, penalty calculations for contract violations, and the use of their names, likenesses, and voices after the contract expires. The five members were aged between 14 and 17 when the agreement was signed in 2022. The paper cited five legal experts who reviewed the agreement, with one Seoul-based entertainment lawyer describing it as unusually aggressive. HYBE disputed several aspects of the report, saying the company had complied with child-protection laws and had not forced NewJeans members to leave school or undergo cosmetic procedures.

In its statement, the association said the fairness and legality of an exclusive contract should not be judged based on individual clauses alone, but together with supplementary agreements, relevant laws, the circumstances in which the contract was signed, and how it was actually implemented. It pointed to Korea's standard contract for pop culture artists and the Popular Culture and Arts Industry Development Act, saying both were designed to balance artists' rights with the legitimate interests of agencies that invest heavily in training and developing performers.

The group added that protections for underage trainees have continued to expand, citing supplementary agreements covering privacy and dignity as well as sleep, education, and rest, along with the designation of youth-protection officers at major entertainment companies. It defended the trainee system, arguing it should not be reduced to being labelled as oppressive control, and described it as a talent-development structure with its own characteristics and competitiveness that cannot be judged solely through a Western perspective. The group also expressed concern that details from a contract involved in an ongoing legal dispute had been disclosed overseas despite confidentiality obligations between the parties.

items.headline: Sooyoon Discusses Crafting ‘Sonagi’ and Reconnecting With Fans
items.dek: The songwriter behind Lovely Runner's ‘Sonagi’ talks about the sudden shower that became one of Asia's most requested songs.
body: When K-pop songwriter and musician Sooyoon took on the assignment to write a song for a fictional band in a Korean drama, all he was given was a premise: it needed to fit both heartbreaking and hopeful moments. He had no idea the song ‘Sonagi,’ or Sudden Shower, sung by the fictional group ECLIPSE in the hit K-drama Lovely Runner, would become the massive, much-loved hit that it is today.

Sooyoon, a former member of the K-pop rock band Royal Pirates, built the track around the metaphor of a sudden shower. Rain usually feels sad, he explained, but he wanted the song to show what comes after the rain, when every bad thing washes away, the air turns fresh, and rainbows appear. He used the rain as love falling down all of a sudden.

Despite writing the track in advance without knowing anything about the full drama at all, Sooyoon still somehow captured the exact emotional core of the series through the song. It went on to land on the Billboard charts, be performed on major awards shows, and remain one of the most requested songs across Asia.

His musical journey spans several eras of K-pop and a mix of international influences. Raised in California, he grew up listening to R&B, American and British rock, J-pop, and early K-pop. After Royal Pirates disbanded, he moved into writing tracks for real-world groups like Kep1er, JO1, NEXZ, and P1Harmony alongside longtime collaborator Moon Kim. He describes writing for idol groups as stepping into a different persona, since his own solo tracks lean toward chill, easy-listening melodies, while idol songs call for high energy, heavy rhythms, and broad, open-ended lyrics.

The viral success of Sonagi reignited his desire to perform live and connect directly with fans again. Following his recent visit to Manila in September, where he performed as a guest artist and enjoyed the warm hospitality, and Jollibee's Peach Mango Pie, he is now expanding his solo footprint across Asia. With a concert in Japan recently finished and an acoustic live set with James Lee in Tokyo coming up for his birthday, he hopes to visit more countries soon, including the Philippines. He also has an upcoming release featuring his former Royal Pirates bandmate James Lee, their first official collaboration since their band days.
items.socialCaption: The man behind ‘Sonagi’ had no idea his sudden shower would become a Lovely Runner classic. Sooyoon opens up about the song, his journey, and Manila.

items.dek: Suho, D.O., Chanyeol, Sehun, and Kai closed EXO's sixth tour where it began, at the KSPO Dome in Seoul.
body: Of EXO's 12 members, only Suho, D.O., Chanyeol, Sehun, and Kai took the stage at the KSPO Dome on November 8 to finish the band's sixth tour, EXhOrizon, at the same venue where it began. Nearly 15 years after the group debuted as 12 young men with their own superpowers, the five proved why they are still hailed as the Kings of K-pop.

Some 33,000 fans were there across the three-day Seoul finale from November 6 to 8, many of whom had followed the group for all 14 years. It was a fitting end to a tour that kicked off at the same venue in April before travelling across 14 regions for 27 shows, and seven months later the journey came full circle.

The group opened with ‘Crown,’ a track from its latest album, Reverxe, as the five members descended from the ceiling while a massive ring-shaped display showing a crown rose above the stage. Kai, dressed in a prince-style jacket, called out to EXO-L, the collective name for EXO fans, and the trip through the group's history began with ‘Monster.’ They then slowed things down with ‘Moonlight Shades’ and ‘24/7,’ showing off their vocals, before a medley of the hits that made them a K-pop powerhouse: ‘Tempo,’ ‘Lotto,’ ‘Ko Ko Bop,’ and ‘Call Me Baby.’

A segment called Club Time turned the concert into a rave, with ‘Lucky One,’ ‘Power,’ and ‘Don't Fight the Feeling’ building up to ‘Run,’ which the members performed three times at the fans' request, jumping and running across the stage each time. Later, with the cold weather settling in, they treated the crowd to their signature winter songs, ‘Sing for You,’ ‘For Life,’ ‘Universe,’ and the fan favourite ‘The First Snow.’ They closed the main set with ‘History,’ ‘Love Me Right,’ and ‘Growl,’ then returned for an encore of ‘Paradise,’ ‘Tender Love,’ and ‘Peter Pan.’

The night was full of gratitude on both sides. The members invited fans to sing along to every track and traded jokes between performances, visibly moved as they listened to the audience sing. Chanyeol said the tour reminded him how happy he is to see fans' faces from the stage and hear his fellow members' voices, and promised they would come back with an even better version of themselves. D.O. called the final night one he would remember for the rest of his life, Kai said he would carry the happiness from the moment through their upcoming activities, and Sehun teased upcoming unit activities with Kai starting from the following week. EXO made its comeback in January with its eighth full-length album, Reverxe, its first release in two years and six months, which became its eighth million-selling album.

source.title: How K-pop is lifting wine’s fortunes in Korea

items.headline: K-pop is helping lift wine’s fortunes in Korea
items.dek: A celebrity wine recommendation that sold out in convenience stores is just one sign of how K-pop's reach is reshaping Korea's wine market.
body: Wine is finding a new audience in South Korea, and celebrity posts are helping it get there. A new report from The Drinks Business looks at how social media moments from Korean stars, paired with bottles on convenience store shelves, have given the country's wine market a lift.

The report opens with a July video from actress Lee Min-jung, who teamed up with rapper Jung Han-hae to recommend six white wines for the summer heat. One of her picks was Better Half, a Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc imported by Nara Cellar and listed at 19,900 won. The video has drawn more than 112,000 views, and the importer says convenience store sales of the bottle rose straight after it went up.

Patrick Han, a brand strategy manager at Nara Cellar, said the moment showed how a celebrity recommendation can reach people who would never set foot in a wine shop. Convenience stores, he added, give those fans an easy way to try a bottle, and a good, fairly priced wine can turn that first try into lasting demand.

The change has deeper roots. Wine was long treated as an imported luxury in Korea, held back by a complicated tax system. When the pandemic kept people home, supermarkets and convenience stores began stocking wine, and younger drinkers started picking up bottles on their way home. Import volume jumped 42.7 percent between 2020 and 2021, and import value climbed 76 percent to 570 million dollars by 2022.

Figures for the first eight months of 2026 already sit above pre-pandemic levels, at around 270 million dollars. The report also credits a wider effect it calls the K-halo: as Korean music, film and food travel further around the world, brands that win over Korean shoppers gain attention far beyond the country.
items.socialCaption: A K-drama star's wine pick sold out in convenience stores, and it's part of a much bigger story about K-pop's halo effect on Korea's wine scene. 🍷
items.seoDescription: A Drinks Business report shows how celebrity posts and convenience store sales are lifting Korea's wine market, with imports already above pre-pandemic levels in 2026.

items.headline: Korea Popmusic Industry Association Criticizes NYT Report on NewJeans Contract
items.dek: The industry body says the New York Times turned one group's contract dispute into a verdict on all of K-pop.
body: South Korea's music industry body has pushed back against a New York Times report on NewJeans' contract, saying the newspaper took one group's dispute and turned it into a verdict on K-pop as a whole.

The Korea Popmusic Industry Association, whose members include HYBE, SM, JYP and YG, issued its statement on Monday, November 9. It said the Times report did not give enough weight to the legality of contracts signed under South Korean law, or to the training system that helped turn K-pop into a global industry.

The Times reported on November 5 that it had obtained copies of the exclusive contracts the five NewJeans members signed with ADOR in 2022, when they were aged between 14 and 17. The paper said the contracts left out protections for minors' health, education and rest that appear in the government's standard contract, and quoted legal experts who viewed some terms as unfavourable to the singers.

The association said it regretted that the newspaper had treated a single contract as evidence of a structural problem across the industry, without acknowledging regulatory progress or the industry's own efforts to improve. It also raised concern that details from a contract at the centre of an ongoing legal dispute had been made public through foreign media, despite confidentiality obligations between the parties.

HYBE and ADOR had already responded to the report, saying the leaked contracts were being used to attack the K-pop industry. The dispute behind it dates back to 2024, when the members announced they were ending their contracts with ADOR; a Seoul court upheld the contracts' validity in October 2025.
items.socialCaption: K-pop's industry body is pushing back on the NYT's NewJeans contract report, saying one group's dispute shouldn't define the whole industry.

body: A South Korean music industry association has warned against treating the NewJeans contract dispute as a problem with all of K-pop, after a New York Times report examined the group's deal with ADOR.

The Korea Popmusic Industry Association said the Times report judged K-pop contracts through too narrow a lens. In its statement, the group argued that the fairness of a contract cannot be decided from single clauses alone, and should be weighed alongside supplementary agreements, the relevant laws, the circumstances of the signing and how the deal was actually carried out.

The association also stressed that the rights of minors must be protected, and pointed out that major companies, including HYBE, sign trainee agreements as well as the national standard youth annexe, which covers personality rights, sleep, education and rest. It said the training system behind K-pop, built on years of investment in young artists, deserved to be understood on its own terms rather than judged only through a Western lens.

The Times report, published on November 5, was based on copies of the exclusive contracts the five members of NewJeans signed with ADOR in 2022, when they were aged 14 to 17. The paper said the documents omitted some protections for minors found in the government's standard contract.

The association added that it was deeply concerned the contents of a contract under legal dispute had been disclosed through foreign media. HYBE and ADOR have also criticised the leak, saying the agreements were being used as a means to attack the K-pop industry.

source.title: Small agencies launch 90% of K-pop groups, but struggle to keep them alive: study

items.headline: Study Finds Small Agencies Launch 90% of K-Pop Groups
items.dek: Small agencies launch nearly nine in ten K-pop groups, but their acts last about half as long as those from the majors.
body: Small agencies launch almost every K-pop group, but they rarely get to keep them. A new study of more than 1,100 idol groups has put numbers on a gap the industry has long talked about.

The study, led by Professor Kim Jung-seop of Sungshin Women's University and published in the Journal of the Korea Entertainment Industry Association, looked at 1,159 groups that debuted between 1996 and 2025. Of those, 1,042, or 89.9 percent, came from small and mid-sized agencies, while just 117 debuted under the major companies.

The difference shows up in how long groups last. Acts from major agencies stayed active for an average of 7.4 years, more than double the 3.6 years managed by groups from smaller companies. Five years after debut, 65.2 percent of major-agency groups were still active, compared with just 28.7 percent of the rest. After ten years, the figures stood at 49.8 percent against 13.2 percent.

The study counted HYBE, SM, JYP, YG, CJ ENM and Kakao, along with their subsidiaries, as major agencies. It also found that the share of groups selling at least a million copies of a single album was more than 30 times higher for major-agency acts.

Kim proposed ten policy measures to help smaller agencies, including investment funds tied to intellectual property, digital marketing support and help with overseas showcases. The message of the study is that the industry needs support for keeping groups alive after debut, not just for launching new ones.
items.socialCaption: Small agencies launch 90% of K-pop groups, but most of those groups don't survive. A new study shows just how wide the gap really is.
items.seoDescription: A study of 1,159 K-pop groups finds small agencies launch 89.9% of them, but their acts stay active about half as long as groups from major companies.

TOMORROW X TOGETHER follow on November 16 with their ninth mini album, PERFECT STORM, which carries six new tracks and another chapter of the Star Seekers lore that runs through their work. The release lands just ahead of the group's fifth world tour, Steal The Wind, so the story is set to move from record to stage.

ENHYPEN bring their THE SIN series to a close on November 20 with the three-track spinoff single THE SIN: PARALLEL WORLD, their third comeback of the year. The title track, I Want You, turns the series' grand themes into a story about fate and connection between two people.

Yves rounds out the same day with her fifth EP, Cute & Anxiety, a record whose title pairs two feelings that rarely sit together. Two pre-release tracks arrived on October 27: Hysteric, built on a dark house groove, and Adam, which leans more experimental and spacey.

items.headline: Stanford to Offer BTS-Inspired Well-Being Program
items.dek: Stanford University is offering a freshman seminar built around "Namjooning," the fan term for BTS leader RM's slow-living habits.
body: A fan-coined word for BTS leader RM's favourite pastimes is now the name of a course at Stanford University. The school is offering 'Namjooning, and Other Well-Being Inspiration from BTS,' a three-unit freshman seminar that uses RM's everyday habits as a starting point for studying mental health.

'Namjooning' is the term fans use for the slower, more reflective activities RM is known for: visiting museums, reading, cycling and spending time in nature. The course, listed as PSYC 65N, runs through the autumn 2026 term, from September 22 to December 4, and is taught by James R. Jacobs, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences who also serves as Stanford's associate vice provost for health and well-being.

The seminar looks at topics from sleep and anxiety to creative blocks, self-love, self-awareness, diet, exercise and psychotherapy, along with art and literature. Students read fiction and scientific papers, study artworks and watch videos, including material that follows RM's creative journey.

The approach is deliberately evidence-based. Rather than simply copying RM's habits, students are asked to weigh what research actually shows about each practice, including how much sleep people need and whether naps help. Their final project takes its inspiration from RM's 2022 solo album, Indigo.
The course arrives months after BTS played sold-out shows at Stanford Stadium in May 2026, a visit that also led to a separate summer K-pop course through Stanford Continuing Studies.

body: Channel A’s “kiDnap GAME” has released new stills ahead of episode 6, as its survival game takes another turn for characters played by Lee Joon Gi and Sakaguchi Kentaro.

The closing show opened with 'Crown' and 'Suffocate' from the group's latest album, Reverxe, alongside their 2016 hit 'Monster,' and the members held their live vocals steady through demanding choreography for about three hours. items.headline: 6 Chinese Workplace Dramas About Women Finding Their Own Paths
items.dek: From consulting to law and entrepreneurship, these dramas follow women balancing career ambitions with personal challenges.
body: Workplace dramas can put more than office rivalries in the spotlight. These six Chinese series follow women making decisions about their careers, relationships and futures, whether they are navigating a demanding employer or starting a business of their own.

The Rational Life
Qin Lan plays Shen Ruo Xin, a senior manager in an automobile company’s legal department who faces gender discrimination at work and pressure to marry at home. When optimistic intern Qi Xiao (Dylan Wang) enters her life, his support prompts her to reconsider her views on relationships while she continues to make choices for herself.

Nothing But Thirty
Set in Shanghai, this drama follows three women as they enter their thirties. Luxury saleswoman Wang Man Ni (Maggie Jiang) hopes to build a better life, Gu Jia (Tong Yao) balances family responsibilities with helping run her husband’s fireworks business, and Zhong Xiao Qin (Mao Xiao Tong) reassesses her choices amid marital difficulties. Their intersecting stories explore ambition, financial independence and friendship.

Irreplaceable
Zhao Jin Mai stars as Xu Chi, a newcomer determined to prove herself in the competitive consulting industry. Elite consultant Ye Xin Zhi (Wei Da Xun), who is dealing with the fallout of a former superior’s betrayal, becomes her mentor. Their relationship develops alongside workplace rivalries and career challenges.

As Beautiful As You
After growing frustrated with her job, technology professional Ji Xing (Tan Song Yun) leaves to launch a medical technology start-up. Building the company brings setbacks, but she eventually gains the backing of investor Han Ting (Xu Kai). Their partnership turns romantic, even as Ji Xing remains intent on pursuing her goals on her own terms.

Love Has Fireworks
Investment banker Qian Fei (Wang Chu Ran) must rethink her future after her fiancé leaves her and she is left with a mortgage. She rents a room to Li Yi Fei (Tan Jian Ci), another investment banking professional, to ease the financial strain. The pair initially clash, but grow closer as they share a home and work on projects together.

She and Her Perfect Husband
Career-focused lawyer Qin Shi (Yang Mi) becomes a candidate for a position at a law firm that requires applicants to be married, unaware that her brother has falsely listed her as a wife. She later meets Yang Hua (Xu Kai), and the two agree to marry. Their arrangement brings professional and family pressures into focus as their relationship develops.

source.title: 'Taken for granted': When K-pop stars lose devoted supporters

items.headline: The Korea Times Examines K-pop Stars Losing Devoted Fans
items.dek: Two longtime fan pages closed within days of each other, both pointing to the same complaint: poor communication and too little respect.
body: Two of K-pop's most loyal fan communities have walked away within days of each other, and the reasons they gave sound strikingly similar. A major fan page for T.O.P, active since his debut in 2006, announced it was shutting down after 20 years, and a fan page for singer Heo Young-saeng said it was ending 16 years of activity. In both cases, the supporters said they felt ignored and taken for granted.

The operators of the T.O.P fan page said they had ended up doing work they believed belonged to his agency, from helping with album promotion to passing messages between the company and fans. They said the agency repeatedly failed to keep fans updated and shifted its own responsibilities onto them. The page also cancelled a photo exhibition it had planned, citing budget limits and too few reservations, and stressed that the decision had nothing to do with T.O.P's private life.

T.O.P's agency, TOPSPOT PICTURES, later posted an apology on social media, saying it took fans' concerns seriously and would work on communicating better and listening to feedback. T.O.P also posted a long message of his own, thanking the fan page operators and supporters who had stood by him, saying their encouragement had helped him return to music, and apologising to those who had felt hurt or misunderstood.

The Heo Young-saeng fan said they had spent about six months preparing a birthday cafe event at their own expense and had asked the agency in advance whether he could visit. According to the fan, the agency replied that it would be difficult for him to visit only one particular cafe. The fan said Heo then rented a separate venue to meet supporters on his birthday and mentioned the birthday cafe during that gathering in a way that left them feeling embarrassed and dismissed.

Other fans offered a different version of events, sharing a video of Heo attending a cafe gathering after returning from Japan and finishing dance practice. The two closures have sparked wide online discussion, with many sympathising with the exhausted fans while others debated how the situations were handled. The episode is a reminder that fan loyalty is not unconditional, and that long years of support still need honest communication and mutual respect in return.
items.socialCaption: Two veteran fan pages closed in the same week after decades of support. Here's what T.O.P and Heo Young-saeng's longtime fans said went wrong, and how both artists responded.

WME, based in Beverly Hills, represents artists, actors and athletes across music, film, television and other fields, with music clients including Bruno Mars and Rihanna. For Jisoo, the agency will act as her worldwide representative, opening up international opportunities as her solo work grows.

The agreement does not replace any of her current partnerships. She continues to run her solo activities through Blissoo, the label she launched in February 2024, and her global solo record deal with Warner Records, signed in January 2025, stays in place. Her BLACKPINK activities remain under YG Entertainment.

Jisoo is the third BLACKPINK member to sign with WME. Lisa joined the agency in September 2025 for film and television work, while Rosé signed that December for representation across all areas of her music career.

The signing comes as Jisoo prepares her first full-length solo album. She has already released two songs ahead of it, with the first arriving on September 4 and the second, ADDICTED, following on October 30. According to Blissoo, ADDICTED reached No. 1 on iTunes Top Songs charts in 28 regions. The album's title and release date have not been announced yet. Jisoo debuted with BLACKPINK in 2016 and launched her solo career in 2023, and she has also built an acting career, starring in the 2025 series Newtopia and film Omniscient Reader: The Prophecy.

items.headline: BTS’ RM Inspires Stanford Course on Well-Being
items.dek: Stanford's new freshman seminar turns RM's everyday habits, museums, books, bike rides and time in nature, into a serious study of mental health.
body: BTS leader RM has inspired a new course at Stanford University, where students are studying well-being through the everyday habits he is known for. The three-unit freshman seminar is titled Namjooning, and Other Well-Being Inspiration from BTS, and it runs through Stanford's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences for the fall 2026 semester.

Namjooning is a term coined by fans from RM's Korean name, Kim Namjoon. It describes the slower, more reflective activities he enjoys, including visiting museums, reading, cycling and spending time in nature. Rather than focusing on his music or career, the course uses those habits as a starting point for questions about mental health.

Students look at topics ranging from sleep and anxiety to self-awareness, exercise and psychotherapy, along with creative blocks, self-love, diet and nutritional supplements. They read fiction, examine artwork and review scientific papers, with the emphasis on what the evidence actually says about how different activities may affect psychological well-being.

The course is taught by James R. Jacobs, Stanford's associate vice provost for health and well-being and a faculty member in psychiatry and behavioral sciences. According to Stanford, RM is frequently quoted for his approaches to mental health and well-being, which helped inspire the class.

Students also complete a final project inspired by RM's 2022 solo album Indigo. The point is not to treat his lifestyle as a prescription for better mental health, but to test everyday habits against real research and see what holds up.
items.socialCaption: Namjooning is now a Stanford course. The BTS leader's love of museums, books and bike rides is the starting point for a real seminar on sleep, anxiety and well-being.
items.seoDescription: Stanford is offering a freshman seminar called "Namjooning, and Other Well-Being Inspiration from BTS," using RM's habits to explore mental health through scientific research.

The preview opens with the five members enjoying a free-spirited moment on a dark stage as confetti falls around them, with bright lighting cutting through the darkness.

The teaser then shows the group running powerfully toward somewhere, alongside an unidentified presence. The soaring melody heard in that moment blends with the members' footsteps, giving the preview a sense of excitement and forward motion. The scenes of the group sharing time on stage and running together were designed to reflect the song's message of connection and companionship.

With is the title track of RESCENE's fourth mini album, PULSE, which was released on November 3 at 6 p.m. The song reached No. 1 on the Melon TOP100 two hours after release, and all five tracks from the album entered the chart's Top 10. With will play over the ending credits in both the subtitled and dubbed versions of the film in Korea, making RESCENE the first Korean girl group to have a song close out a Disney film.

items.headline: Stanford Offers ‘Namjooning’ Course Inspired by BTS’ RM
items.dek: A Stanford psychology seminar is putting RM's approach to slowing down under a scientific microscope, and asking students to test it, not just admire it.
body: Stanford University is offering an undergraduate course inspired by Kim Namjoon, better known as RM, the leader of BTS. Listed as PSYC 65N and titled Namjooning, and Other Well-Being Inspiration from BTS, the three-unit seminar is open to first-year students and runs in the autumn 2026 term, from September 22 to December 4.

The class takes its name from Namjooning, a fan-created term for the way RM recharges: visiting art museums, reading, cycling, journaling and spending time in nature. Stanford describes RM as someone frequently quoted for his approaches to mental health and well-being, and the course uses those habits as its entry point rather than his music.

But this is not a fan club with course credit. The seminar promises to put every piece of wellness advice under a quantitative microscope, asking not just whether something helps, but how much, for whom, and what the research actually shows. Students examine scientific papers, read fiction, analyse art and watch videos, including material exploring RM's creative journey.

The syllabus covers nature, biking, art and literature, alongside sleep, anxiety and creative blocks, self-love and self-awareness, diet, exercise, nutritional supplements, psychotherapy and coaching. Assignments include short presentations and brief writing work, and the capstone is a final project inspired by Indigo, RM's 2022 solo album.

The class is led by James R. Jacobs, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences who also serves as Stanford's associate vice provost for health and well-being. Its prerequisites are memorable in themselves: students need a desire to flourish at Stanford and in life, an appetite for data, and a healthy respect for BTS.

The showing adds to a strong year for K-pop on the big screen in Australia, where concert films have become a regular way for fans to experience tours they could not attend in person. body: JYP Entertainment has confirmed it will debut a new boy band, oftheblue, next year. The company announced the plan on November 9, with the group set to launch in 2027 under SQU4D, the JYP division behind girl group NMIXX.

The debut makes oftheblue the first boy group from SQU4D, and JYP's first new boy group in two years since KickFlip debuted in 2025. SQU4D was set up around Lee Ji-young, JYP's first female inside director, and introduced its first act, NMIXX, in February 2022. The new group is described as the product of the producing and management approach that helped establish NMIXX.

The group's name comes from the English idiom out of the blue, meaning an unexpected moment or discovery. Dropping the word out, the group gives blue the meanings of limitless possibility, freedom and youth, with the stated concept being a portrait of youth full of unpredictable moments.

Promotion is already running, and it leans heavily on mystery. SQU4D opened oftheblue's official social media accounts at midnight KST on November 6 with two images: a portrait with a QR code covering the face, and a crossword with the English words BLIND and BLUE filled in. A group logo followed on November 7, with a flyer-style image on November 8.

The QR code leads to a promotional website filled with sky, sunset, field and tidal-shore scenes, along with city objects such as a camcorder, an MP3 player and earphones. The site also includes film photos the members shot around Seoul and a digital mixer with 18 everyday sounds, including footsteps on sand, that visitors can layer into their own mix. The lineup and exact debut date have not been announced, and the four men visible on the promotional site have fuelled fan guesses about a four-member lineup, but no official member count has been given.

items.headline: Former PENTAGON Member Yan An Builds Acting Career
items.dek: A decade after debuting with PENTAGON, Yan An is now leading a Chinese costume drama, his first major starring role.
body: Yan An is steadily building a second career as an actor in China, a decade after first making his name in K-pop. The Chinese singer and actor debuted in South Korea in 2016 as a member of boy group PENTAGON, serving as the group's vocalist and visual after coming through a survival show run by Cube Entertainment.

After taking a hiatus due to health issues and seeing his contract with Cube expire in 2023, he chose to return to China to pursue his career there. His acting work began in 2021, when he took on the role of Shi Junjie in the Chinese drama Use for My Talent, his first step into screen acting.

His profile rose sharply in 2024, when he played Li Lun, a thousand-year-old demon, in the fantasy drama Fangs of Fortune. The role put his name on the map with Chinese drama viewers and marked a turning point in how he was seen, from idol-turned-actor to a performer in his own right. He followed it with another supporting role in Veil of Shadows.

Now, as he marks his tenth anniversary in showbiz, Yan An has taken on his first major leading role. He plays the male lead, Lu Zhuo, in the costume drama Where the Mask Ends, opposite Tian Xiwei. The series follows a substitute bride and a marriage-first, love-later story, and it quickly passed 9,000 on Youku's heat index after its premiere.

The move from group vocalist to drama lead has been gradual rather than sudden, built project by project over five years. With a leading role now under his belt, Yan An's screen career has moved from supporting parts into the spotlight.

items.headline: Ticketing day, minus the panic
items.dek: The checklist to finish before a Philippine K-pop ticket sale opens, so the queue is the only thing left to worry about.
body: A ticket sale is won before it opens. The fans who get in are usually the ones who did the boring prep the night before, and this guide is that prep, in order.

Start with the official seller. Every Philippine show on the HallyuScope concert calendar links to the exact official ticketing page, and the sellers are the same names every time: Ticketmaster PH, SM Tickets, TicketNet, Tap Your Tickets, and Megatix. If a link is not one of those, or not the promoter's own page, do not trust it. Resellers and random social media sellers are where fans lose money.

Make the account the night before. Create an account on the seller's site, save your payment method, and log in once so you know the password works. SM Tickets runs a queue system, so expect a waiting room and do not refresh it. Ticketmaster PH and TicketNet also queue during big sales, and refreshing usually sends you to the back of the line.

Know the sale time in Manila time. Sales open at a specific hour, and the big ones sell out fast. KATSEYE's Manila general sale opened November 13, after presales on November 10 to 12. DOH KYUNG SOO's Manila tickets went on sale November 20 at 2 PM. The calendar lists the sale date for every show, so check it before the day.

Have a backup plan, not a backup seller. Decide your section and your price ceiling before the queue opens, so you are not deciding while the clock runs. If your first choice sells out, take the next best seat in the same sale rather than chasing a second site. And keep the confirmation email and the ticket QR somewhere you can reach them without signal, because venue gates are not kind to dead batteries.

body: Your first K-pop concert in Manila is equal parts show and logistics, and the logistics are the part nobody warns you about. This is the short version of what to know before the day.

The shows are mostly in the same venues. SM Mall of Asia Arena in Pasay hosts the biggest tours, Smart Araneta Coliseum in Quezon City hosts the mid-size ones, and New Frontier Theater, Aliw Theater, SM North EDSA Skydome, FYM Hall, and Music Museum cover the rest. Check the venue on the calendar before you plan the trip, because the same artist can play a different venue each tour.

Evening shows start between 5 and 8 PM, and doors usually open an hour or two before that. Leave early. Manila traffic does not care about your lightstick, and the queues for entry, merch, and the official lightstick booth are all longer than you expect. Bring a valid ID and your ticket, digital or printed, and keep both where you can reach them.

The lightstick is the uniform. If the group has one, bring it, charged, with spare batteries. The crowd will do the rest: fan chants during the songs, banners during the ballads, and a sea of light during the encore. If you do not know the chants, listen for a song or two first. Nobody minds a quiet first-timer, and everyone minds a camera flash in a dark arena.

After the show, the venue empties slowly. Plan your ride home before the encore, not after it. Ride hailing surges around the arena, so a pre-booked car or a meetup point a short walk away saves the wait. And keep your ticket stub. First concerts become the one you measure every other concert against.

items.headline: Album versions, POBs and inclusions
items.dek: A plain-language breakdown of versions, pre-order benefits, and what actually comes inside a K-pop album.
body: A K-pop album is not one product. It is a set of versions, each with different covers, different photocards, and sometimes different extras, and the pre-order benefit is a whole second layer on top. Here is what each part means.

Versions are the choices. Most releases come in two or more versions, usually a different cover and a different photocard set per version. Some are member versions, where each version is dedicated to one member. Buying every version is a collector's choice, not a requirement. One version gets you the album, the songs, and a full set of inclusions.

POB stands for pre-order benefit. It is an extra photocard, or a small set of extras, given only to fans who order before the release date, and only from the shop that offers it. Each shop has its own POB, so the same album pre-ordered from two shops comes with two different extra photocards. That is why fans compare shops before they buy.

Inclusions are what comes inside the album. The standard set is a photobook, a CD, and a random photocard, plus extras that change by release: a poster, stickers, a lyrics booklet, or a postcard. The random photocard is the part fans trade. It is one member out of the group, pulled at random, and trading is half the hobby.

Where you buy matters. Official shops and the group's own store are the safe baseline. Local Philippine sellers, both online shops and physical stores, often carry the same versions and run group orders that split shipping. Check the version name, the shop's POB, and the release date before you pay, and keep the order confirmation until the album is in your hands.
